document.title: IIR [Excised] Pakistan Involvement in Afghanistan
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Confidential] ISI is heavily involved in Afghanistan. Pakistan's Pashtun-based Frontier Corps is used for command and control, training and combat in Taliban operations, while the Punjabi-dominated regular army is not. Frontier Corps provide training in Kandahar or Herat to Pakistani madrassa students fighting for the Taliban.

events.description: Intelligence information report to DIA on Pakistani involvement in Afghanistan and Taliban recruitment and training.
Mullah Borjan was shot and killed several days after a quarrel with Rabbani over the fate of a captive in the battle for Kabul (details garbled).

Mullah Borjan was shot and killed several days after a dispute with Rabbani over Hekmatyar's fate. Some senior Taliban leaders blame Rabbani for his death; the text links Borjan to the battle for Kabul.

Rabbani and Borjan had a heated conversation. Borjan ordered that Hekmatyar be arrested and given a fair trial; Rabbani strongly disagreed because Hekmatyar had allegedly murdered his father and brother.
Bashar was in Quetta about two weeks before the report and was believed to be in Herat, Kandahar or Dubai at the time of reporting.

Intelligence report to DIA that two Pakistani madrasas supply most Taliban fighters, that the ISI is heavily involved in Afghanistan, and that Pakistani officials coordinate activities in Afghan provinces.

sources_cited: Intelligence Information Report from a [excised] source to DIA Washington, 7 Nov 1996
key_claims: Two Pakistani madrasas produce most Taliban fighters.
Pakistan's Frontier Corps commandos and former Najibullah-era and Hekmatyar personnel train Taliban recruits for 15-25 days in Kandahar or Herat.
ISI is heavily involved in Afghanistan, with its officers serving as consul generals in Herat and Kandahar.
The Governor of Balochistan coordinates Pakistani activities in the southwestern Afghan provinces.
The report indicates a wealthy Pashtun, Bashar, financed the early Taliban.
